concepts.title: Bounded-Buffer Problem (Semaphore Solution)
concepts.definition: A classical synchronization problem where a producer and a consumer share a fixed buffer of size $n$. It is synchronized using three semaphores: a binary semaphore `mutex` (initialized to 1) for mutual exclusion on buffer access, a counting semaphore `empty` (initialized to $n$) tracking available slots, and a counting semaphore `full` (initialized to 0) tracking occupied slots. The producer executes `wait(empty)`, `wait(mutex)`, produces, `signal(mutex)`, `signal(full)`; the consumer executes `wait(full)`, `wait(mutex)`, consumes, `signal(mutex)`, `signal(empty)`.
concepts.evidence:
Semaphore mutex initialized to the value 1
Semaphore full initialized to the value 0
Semaphore empty initialized to the value n
useWhen: Coordinating producer and consumer processes sharing a fixed-size buffer using semaphores

concepts.title: Readers-Writers Problem
concepts.definition: A classical synchronization problem involving a data set shared among concurrent processes where readers only read data without modifying it and writers can both read and write. The synchronization requirement is that multiple readers may read simultaneously, but only a single writer may access the shared data exclusively at any given time.
concepts.evidence:
Problem – allow multiple readers to read at the same time
Only one single writer can access the shared data at the same time

concepts.title: First and Second Readers-Writers Problem Variations
concepts.definition: Variations of the readers-writers problem based on priority: In the first readers-writers problem, no reader is kept waiting unless a writer has already obtained permission to use the shared object (which can starve writers). In the second readers-writers problem, once a writer is ready, no newly arrived reader may start reading, prioritizing writers (which can starve readers).
concepts.evidence:
The solution in previous slide can result in a situation where a writer process never writes. It is referred to as the “First reader-writer” problem.
The “Second reader-writer” problem is a variation the first reader-writer problem that state:
Once a writer is ready to write, no “newly arrived reader” is allowed to read.

concepts.title: Dining-Philosophers Problem
concepts.definition: A classical synchronization problem modeling resource allocation among $N$ processes (philosophers) seated around a table who alternate between thinking and eating. Eating requires acquiring two shared adjacent resources (chopsticks), picked up one at a time. A naive semaphore solution where every philosopher simultaneously picks up their left chopstick leads to deadlock.
concepts.evidence:
N philosophers’ sit at a round table with a bowel of rice in the middle.
They spend their lives alternating thinking and eating.
They do not interact with their neighbors.
Occasionally try to pick up 2 chopsticks (one at a time) to eat from bowl
Need both to eat, then release both when done

concepts.title: Dining-Philosophers Monitor Solution
concepts.definition: A deadlock-free solution to the dining-philosophers problem implemented inside a monitor. Each philosopher tracks their state as `THINKING`, `HUNGRY`, or `EATING`. A philosopher may transition to `EATING` only if neither neighbor is currently eating (`state[(i+4)%5] != EATING && state[(i+1)%5] != EATING`). If chopsticks are unavailable, the philosopher invokes `wait()` on a condition variable `self[i]`. When putting down chopsticks, a philosopher tests both neighbors to signal them if they are waiting and eligible to eat. This eliminates deadlock, though starvation is still possible.
useWhen: Designing a deadlock-free dining-philosophers solution using monitors and condition variables

concepts.title: Windows Dispatcher Objects
concepts.definition: Kernel synchronization mechanisms in Windows available to user-space threads, encompassing mutexes, semaphores, events, and timers. Dispatcher objects exist in either a signaled state (the object is available, allowing an acquiring thread to proceed without blocking) or a non-signaled state (the object is unavailable, causing an acquiring thread to block).
concepts.evidence:
Also provides dispatcher objects user-land which may act mutexes, semaphores, events, and timers
Dispatcher objects either signaled-state (object available) or non-signaled state (thread will block)

concepts.title: POSIX Named vs. Unnamed Semaphores
concepts.definition: POSIX provides semaphores in two forms: named semaphores, which have a name in the filesystem and can be shared and accessed by unrelated processes, and unnamed semaphores, which reside in memory and can only be used by threads of the same process or processes sharing memory.
concepts.evidence:
POSIX provides two versions – named and unnamed.
Named semaphores can be used by unrelated processes, unnamed cannot.

concepts.title: POSIX Condition Variables
concepts.definition: Synchronization primitives in POSIX (Pthreads) that allow threads to block until a specific predicate is satisfied. Because C and C++ lack built-in monitor language constructs, every POSIX condition variable (`pthread_cond_t`) is explicitly associated with a POSIX mutex lock (`pthread_mutex_t`) to ensure mutual exclusion while checking conditions and waiting.
concepts.evidence: Since POSIX is typically used in C/C++ and these languages do not provide a monitor, POSIX condition variables are associated with a POSIX mutex lock to provide mutual exclusion
useWhen: Synchronizing threads in C/C++ under POSIX based on conditional state changes

concepts.title: Java Monitors
concepts.definition: Java's language-level synchronization mechanism where every object has an associated intrinsic lock and two thread queues: an entry set and a wait set. Calling a `synchronized` method requires acquiring the object's lock; if unavailable, the thread joins the entry set. Inside synchronized code, calling `wait()` releases the lock and places the thread into the wait set; calling `notify()` selects an arbitrary thread from the wait set, moves it to the entry set, and marks it runnable to compete for the lock.
concepts.evidence:
Every Java object has associated with it a single lock.
If a method is declared as synchronized , a calling thread must own the lock for the object.
Locks are released when the owning thread exits the synchronized method.

concepts.title: Java Condition Variables
concepts.definition: Explicit condition synchronization objects created from an instance of `java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock` via `newCondition()`. Threads suspend execution by calling `await()` (which atomically releases the lock) and resume waiting threads by calling `signal()` or `signalAll()`, allowing multiple independent wait-conditions per explicit lock.
concepts.evidence:
Condition variables are associated with an ReentrantLock.
Creating a condition variable using newCondition () method of ReentrantLock :
A thread waits by calling the await() method, and signals by calling the signal() method.
useWhen: Implementing multiple conditional waiting queues on an explicit Java ReentrantLock

concepts.title: Transactional Memory
concepts.definition: A synchronization approach where a sequence of memory read-write operations is executed as an atomic transaction (e.g., within an `atomic { S }` block). If all operations in the transaction complete without conflict from other threads, the transaction commits; if a conflict occurs, changes are aborted and rolled back, and the transaction is retried.
concepts.evidence: A memory transaction is a sequence of read-write operations to memory that are performed atomically. A transaction can be completed by adding atomic{S} which ensure statements in S are executed atomically

concepts.title: OpenMP Critical Section Directive
concepts.definition: A compiler directive in OpenMP written as `#pragma omp critical` that designates the immediately following structured block of code as a critical section, ensuring it is executed by only one thread at a time atomically.
concepts.evidence: The code contained within the #pragma omp critical directive is treated as a critical section and performed atomically.
useWhen: Enforcing mutual exclusion in shared-memory parallel programs written with OpenMP

concepts.title: Functional Programming for Data Races
concepts.definition: A programming paradigm that eliminates data races and synchronization conflicts by treating variables as immutable and maintaining no shared mutable state. Because values cannot change once assigned, concurrent reads never conflict.
concepts.evidence:
Functional programming languages offer a different paradigm than procedural languages in that they do not maintain state.
Variables are treated as immutable and cannot change state once they have been assigned a value.
There is increasing interest in functional languages such as Erlang and Scala for their approach in handling data races.
